USA.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Keep the existing Section 301 tariffs in place and continue the April endgame talks without new tariff hikes, rollbacks, or a purchases-only settlement. Push for written, enforceable text on IP, forced tech transfer, and snap-back enforcement, and treat any Chinese purchase pledges as a complement—not a substitute—for those structural chapters. Hold a Trump–Xi summit only after the text is closed; do not trade away List 3 leverage to force a date.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: Threat is a modest opportunity, not a crisis. The United States already covers ~$250B of Chinese imports (Lists 1–3) while the planned List 3 hike to 25% remains suspended after the 1 Dec 2018 G20 truce and the 24 Feb 2019 delay, so leverage is intact without a new escalation. Intensive Washington talks through 3 Apr 2019 and subsequent Mnuchin/Lighthizer comments show progress on enforcement offices and chapter text, with Trump saying on 4 Apr that remaining issues (IP/theft and the fate of tariffs) would be known within about four weeks—i.e., the dispute is in a negotiation window, not a breakdown. US macro conditions do not show a trade-war recession: VIX ~13, Michigan sentiment 97.2, and CPI contained, even as industrial production has slipped and customs imports from China are down ~26% from late-2018 levels. The real cost is concentrated: China’s 25% soybean tariff has nearly shut a ~$12B market, USDA flagged ~27.5 million tons unsold and ~$7.9B of farm losses, which is politically material but not economy-wide. China, meanwhile, needed a large Q1 credit impulse to print 6.4% GDP and an 8.5% March IP bounce, so Beijing still has reason to close a deal. Escalating tariffs now would likely collapse talks that both sides describe as near an endgame and deepen farm-belt damage; conceding a tariff rollback or locking in state-directed purchases (the $1T-scale lists discussed in early April) before enforcement and IP text is finished would waste the leverage that produced those talks. Hence action_score 0 / negotiate: stay at the table, keep current duties as the enforcement backstop, and refuse both a premature hike and a premature climb-down. The residual risk is a weak deal that waters down industrial-subsidy language (already reported mid-April) while leaving Huawei/Meng and Canadian detentions as a parallel security track—another reason not to rush into concession.
key_factors: Section 301 coverage of ~$250B remains in force; List 3 still at 10% after G20 and Feb 24 delays
April 2019 Washington talks in endgame: enforcement offices largely agreed, IP/tariff-removal still open, no signed deal
US macro resilient (low VIX, solid sentiment) while IMPCH and industrial production show trade friction, not collapse
Concentrated farm-belt pain (soybean market largely shut; USDA unsold-stock and loss estimates) creates political pressure to deal but not to fold
China Q1 2019 stabilization via stimulus reduces panic on their side but still gives them incentive to settle
Risk of a purchases-heavy, subsidy-light deal if the US trades away tariff leverage too early

sources_cited.excerpt: List 3 takes effect at 10%. China imposes retaliatory tariffs (5–10%) on ~$60B of US goods. Combined US Section 301 coverage now ~$250B of Chinese imports.
G20 Buenos Aires dinner: Trump and Xi agree to a 90-day negotiation window. Planned Jan 1, 2019 hike of List 3 from 10% to 25% is suspended.
Trump tweets that talks have made substantial progress and further delays the scheduled List 3 hike from 10% to 25%.
Intensive Washington talks between US and Chinese negotiators; both sides report progress on text, including enforcement language. No final deal signed.
VIX latest 13.14 on 2019-04-24, down sharply from late-2018 stress levels — markets not pricing a trade-war crisis.
Michigan consumer sentiment 97.2 in April 2019 after a January dip — household confidence recovered during the truce.
US goods imports from China fell to ~$34.5B in April 2019 from ~$46.3B in Nov 2018 (−25.6%), showing tariffs are biting bilateral trade.
US industrial production slipped from 104.07 (Nov 2018) to 102.27 (Apr 2019), a modest real-side drag without a collapse.
Mnuchin (10 Apr 2019): sides have ‘pretty much agreed on an enforcement mechanism’ and will establish enforcement offices; important issues remain; no arbitrary deadline.
Trump (4 Apr 2019): remaining sticking points include IP/theft and certain tariffs; ‘we’ll know over the next four weeks’ if there is a deal and a summit.
USDA chief economist: ~27.5 million tons of US soybeans expected unsold in 2019; ~$7.9B farm losses; China dropped from top to fifth soybean buyer.
Mid-April reporting that US negotiators tempered industrial-subsidy demands under Beijing resistance — risk of a structurally thin deal if leverage is spent too soon.
China Q1 2019 GDP +6.4% (above 6.3% consensus); March industrial production +8.5%, helped by stimulus rather than a hard landing.

CHN.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Stay at the table and keep drafting text without new unilateral tariffs, detentions, or purchase locks. Use purchase volumes and limited IP/market-access language as bargaining chips for a path off the existing $250B U.S. duties, and reject any enforcement design that lets Washington snap tariffs back on unilaterally while ours stay down. Do not reopen the Huawei/Meng track inside the trade talks; keep that channel separate so a commercial deal is still reachable in the four-week window Trump described.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: Threat is material but not existential. Combined Section 301 coverage is still ~$250B of our exports (Lists 1–2 at 25%, List 3 at 10%), and U.S. customs imports from China have fallen about 26% from November 2018 to April 2019, confirming the tariff bite on export hubs. Huawei remains under U.S. fraud/sanctions charges and Meng Wanzhou remains in Canadian custody on a U.S. extradition request—firm-level targeting of a national champion, even though the April talks explicitly did not put Huawei on the table. That maps below the +0.5 anchor (major export hit + Huawei) because the acute hike risk has receded: the January List-3 jump to 25% was suspended at Buenos Aires and delayed again on 24 February, Q1 2019 GDP printed 6.4% (above the 6.3% consensus) as stimulus began to work, and VIX is back near 13. Action should therefore be mild. April 3–5 Washington talks produced line-by-line text and both sides reported progress, but enforcement and whether existing U.S. tariffs come off remain the endgame fight; the U.S. Chamber judged China unlikely to accept snapback tariffs unless current duties are removed. Escalating now would invite the postponed 25% hike and waste a window both presidents have signaled they want. Premature purchase commitments or a partial rollback would give away leverage before Washington matches on tariff relief. Negotiate—no new commitments, no new escalation—is the stance that preserves optionality while the text is still open.
key_factors: Existing U.S. Section 301 coverage still ~$250B; List 3 remains at 10% after two delays of the 25% hike
U.S. goods imports from China down ~26% Nov 2018–Apr 2019, confirming export-hub pressure
Huawei/Meng legal track is live but was kept outside April trade talks
April Washington round: progress on text, no deal; enforcement snapback and tariff-removal path still unresolved
Q1 2019 GDP 6.4% beat and stimulus starting to offset 2018–19 slowdown, so threat is contained not existential
Both leaders have publicly signaled they want a deal in coming weeks; escalation would likely collapse that window
